title: Wired, Tired, or Shut Down: A Plain-English Guide to Your Nervous System
excerpt: A jargon-free tour of fight-flight, freeze, and calm — and simple ways to help your body feel safer.

value.text: You have probably noticed that some days you feel revved up and unable to settle, other days flat and heavy and hard to get moving, and — on the good days — simply steady. These are not random moods or character flaws. They are states of your nervous system, and once you can recognise them, a lot of confusing experiences start to make sense.

This is a plain-language tour of that system — no jargon, no requirement to feel anything in particular, just a map. Understanding what your body is doing, and why, is often the first step toward helping it feel safer. And feeling safer, it turns out, is not something you can simply think your way into.

Beneath conscious thought, your nervous system is always scanning: is this safe, or is this too much? It does this faster than you can reason, and it does it constantly — reading tone of voice, the look on a face, the tension in a room. Depending on what it senses, it shifts you into a different state, each one an intelligent attempt to keep you safe. The trouble is not that these states exist; it is that they can get stuck.

When your system reads a demand it thinks you need to meet, it mobilises — the familiar fight-or-flight surge. Heart rate rises, muscles tense, attention narrows, energy floods in. In a genuine emergency this is exactly what you want. The difficulty comes when modern life keeps triggering it — a full inbox, a difficult conversation, a relentless schedule — and it never fully switches off.

Stuck in the wired state, you might feel anxious, on edge, irritable, or unable to relax even when nothing is obviously wrong. Your body is doing its job well; it is simply responding to a threat level that no longer matches your actual life.

When something feels not just demanding but overwhelming or inescapable, the system can do the opposite of mobilise. It powers down — the freeze response. Energy drops, motivation fades, you feel numb, distant, heavy, or strangely blank. From the outside this can look like laziness or low mood; from the inside it is a protective brake, an old response to feeling that there is nothing you can do.

It helps to know that shutdown is not a failure of willpower. You cannot simply decide your way out of it, any more than you can decide your way out of the wired state. Both are your body's doing, and both respond better to gentleness than to force.

There is a third state, and it is the one everything else is trying to protect. When your system senses that you are genuinely safe, it settles. Your breathing eases, your body softens, and — crucially — you can connect. In this state you can think clearly, feel close to others, rest, and recover. This is not the absence of the other states; it is the home base your nervous system is always trying to return to.

Health is not living permanently in calm — that is not how bodies work. It is flexibility: the ability to mobilise when you need to, and then come back to settled when the demand has passed. Difficulty tends to arrive when you get stuck in one state and cannot find the way back.

Because these states live in the body, the ways back tend to be physical rather than purely mental. You are not trying to force calm; you are offering your nervous system small, honest cues of safety and letting it respond in its own time.

items: Slow the out-breath. A longer exhale than inhale is one of the body's clearest signals that it is safe to settle.
Use your senses. Feet on the floor, warmth in your hands, something to look at or hear — orienting to the present tells the body the danger is not here now.
Move to discharge a wired state. A brisk walk lets mobilised energy complete rather than churn.
Add gentle warmth and connection when shut down. Force rarely lifts a freeze; kindness and a small, safe person or place often can.
Go small and slow. More is not better; nervous systems change through gentle, repeated experiences of safety, not big efforts.

value.text: If this map feels useful and you would like to understand the body-based side more deeply, my introduction to [what Somatic Experiencing is](/blog/what-is-somatic-experiencing) picks up exactly where this leaves off. And if you would rather explore your own patterns with support, you can see how I work on the [work together](/work-with-me) page.

The most quietly freeing thing about this map is what it does to self-blame. When you understand that being wired, tired, or shut down is your body protecting you — not a personal failing — you can meet those states with curiosity instead of criticism. And from that gentler place, steadiness has far more room to grow.
